title: Multiworkload kernel interference quant benchmark notes
content:
Context and motivation:
This is a note dump from a short probe we ran to understand how quantized kernels behave under mixed/concurrent workloads. Prior runs focused on single-workload steady-state (microbench-style). Production signals show tail latency and throughput regressions when heterogeneous request mixes hit the same GPU — especially when we mix AWQ-quantized models with INT8- and FP8-compiled variants on the same device. This doc captures the harness, preliminary numbers, hypotheses, and next steps.

High-level hypothesis:
- Kernel selection and per-kernel workspace allocations create contention on shared SM/TensorCore resources.
- Mixed kernels cause scheduler churn (stream syncs and small memcpy stalls) which increases p95/p99 even if aggregate throughput (tokens/sec) stays similar.
- Some quant formats (AWQ) trigger alternate memory access patterns that increase L2 cache miss rates when co-located with INT8 kernels that use packed GEMM lanes.

Experiment setup (short):
- Hardware: 2x A100 (80GB) in single-machine tests. Secondary exploratory run on 1x H100 to validate architecture differences.
- Runtime: serving-runtime branch: probe/multiworkload-2025-09 (WIP).
- Models: open-model-v1-13B (base FP32), quant variants produced via GPTQ, AWQ, and vendor int8 toolchain.
- Kernels: 3 kernel families exercised: gptq-optimized (fused matmul + attention), awq-block-kern, int8-packed-gemm.
- Client mix: three synthetic arrival patterns ran for 30 minutes each:
  - Mix A (50% AWQ-13B, 50% INT8-13B), 100 RPS steady, 16 token output avg.
  - Mix B (25% AWQ, 25% GPTQ, 50% FP8-13B), Poisson bursts: 200 RPS for 60s every 5 min.
  - Single baseline: 100% INT8 at 100 RPS (control).
- Metrics instrumented: p50/p95/p99 token latency, tokens/sec, GPU util (sm, tensor cores), L2 hit/miss, kernel queue times (time between launch and completion), CUDA stream stalls, memcopy bandwidth, and OOM / allocation spikes.

Key results (summary numbers):
- Baseline (100% INT8): tokens/sec = 120k, p95 = 48 ms, p99 = 98 ms. Stable across run.
- Mix A (AWQ + INT8): tokens/sec = 116k (-3.3%), p95 = 82 ms (+71%), p99 = 210 ms (+114%).
- Mix B (tri-mix with FP8 bursts): tokens/sec = 110k (-8.3%), p95 = 95 ms (+98%), p99 = 265 ms (+170%).
- H100 quick check: Mix A still showed p99 regression but smaller magnitude (~+60% vs baseline p99).

Observations from traces and profiler (nsight/trace + runtime logs):
- Increased kernel scheduling gaps: trace shows frequent small gaps (50-200us) between launches for mixed workloads compared to tight launch chains for single-kernel runs.
- CUDA stream synchronization: awq-block-kern uses a fallback that performs small device->device memcopies for rearranged weights which introduces occasional stream sync points. When interleaved with int8-packed launches, these memcopies block shared DMA channels and increase queue latency for subsequent matric multiplications.
- L2 cache behavior: AWQ runs showed higher L2 miss per instruction when colocated. L2 miss spikes align with p99 spikes in trace.
- Workspace allocations: int8-packed-gemm kernel allocates temporary workspace per-call. Under concurrency, our allocator serializes some allocations causing short critical sections.
- Kernel fusion mismatches: GPTQ-fused kernels are longer-running but more bandwidth-friendly; interleaving short high-IO kernels with long compute kernels causes head-of-line blocking in our local stream scheduling (we use per-instance stream assignment that needs revisiting).

Repro attempts and flakiness notes:
- Reproduced most spikes reliably with synthetic mix and no other host noise. Some p99 events depend on alignment of a memcopy + long kernel; randomness in request timing changes exact time but distribution consistent.
- Lowering AWQ batch size reduced contention (thought experiment: smaller AWQ batches mean shorter memcopy windows), but increased overhead of kernel launches and hurt aggregate throughput.

Concrete root-cause candidates (ranked):
1) Stream syncs caused by AWQ weight rearrange memcopies interacting with int8-packed kernel launches (most evidence).
2) Allocator serialization for temporary workspaces (moderate evidence).
3) Kernel resource partitioning: different kernels use SM/TensorCore resources differently; current scheduler doesn't consider kernel resource footprint when interleaving (we schedule round-robin per-request).
4) Cache interference due to different memory access patterns (observational).

Quick mitigations tested locally:
- Policy A: pin quant variant families to separate GPUs (dedicated lanes). Fixes p99 but reduces utilization; tokens/sec drops ~18% for the same machine.
- Policy B: coarse-grained request batching windows aligned per kernel family (batch AWQ requests into a 200ms window). Reduced launch churn and p99 improved by ~40% but introduced higher p50 for AWQ, overall user impact mixed.
- Policy C: pre‑warm workspace allocations with thread-local pools; reduced allocator stalls and improved p95 by ~12% in mixed runs.

Notes on measurement gaps and follow-ups:
- Need microbench for the per-call workspace allocation path to determine lock hold times and possible lock-free alternatives.
- Capture NVLink / PCIe bandwidth counters during mixed runs to ensure memcopy contention is measured at the right layer.
- Add kernel-level tagging in trace (kernel family + quant format) so we can quickly filter p99 events by offending kernel transitions.

Action items (short-term):
- (Aisha) Add kernel family tags to runtime traces and enable for next smoke run (SRV-1408). Target: 2025-09-19.
- (Marcus) Build microbench to exercise allocator path with synthetic concurrency and report lock contention (due 2025-09-23).
- (Diego) Validate stream strategy: prototype dedicated streams per kernel family vs current per-instance streams and measure p99/throughput tradeoffs (due 2025-09-26).
- (Priya) Run NVLink/PCIe counters for Mix A and Mix B on H100 and A100, attach logs to JIRA (due 2025-09-22).

Longer-term ideas (researchy):
- Adaptive scheduling: runtime learns kernel resource footprint (mem vs compute) and groups similar kernels to reduce cache/DMA interference.
- Kernel admission controller: if mixed workload expected, hold small requests for micro-batching to avoid interleaving short I/O-heavy kernels with long compute kernels.
- Compile-time hints: annotate compiled kernels with their expected L2 working set and memcopy behavior so runtime can make smarter placement.

Appendix: quick trace snippets (translated):
- Example: request 1732 (AWQ) launches weight-rearrange memcpy at t=12.324s which holds CUDA memcpy stream until t=12.3247s. Immediately after, int8 kernel launch for request 1733 delayed by 150us waiting on stream resource. That 150us multiplied across many requests produces the observed p99 tail.
- Allocation hot path: allocator lock held for median 8us, 95th 45us under mixed load vs median 2us, 95th 8us in single kernel baseline.

Open questions / discussion points for sync:
- Is separating quant families to different devices acceptable as a short-term mitigation for enterprise customers? Tradeoffs: SLA vs cost.
- Do we prefer runtime-level batching heuristics (more invasive) or micro-optimizations (allocator, stream assignment) first?

References and artifacts: probe deck (in-confluence), SRV-1408 for tracking, PR prototype at github link above.

Raw logs and profiler captures are attached to the JIRA ticket; see linked_artifacts.

Status: drafting runbook-style notes; will convert into a lightweight playbook once remaining microbench data is in (expected 2025-09-26).
